hints: Focus on what excess H2 with Ni does to each C=C bond, it adds one H to each alkene carbon to make it fully saturated.
Remember a chiral carbon needs four different groups, so a new CH2 group can never be chiral but a new CH(CH3) group often can be.
Check each of the three double bonds for how many CH(CH3) centres they create, then add any saturated chiral centre already present in Y.
walkthrough:
**Find what hydrogenation changes**

Think simply, each C=C becomes C-C by adding one H atom to each carbon. Compound Y has three C=C bonds, so six carbons change from planar sp2 to tetrahedral sp3.

$$\text{C=C} + \text{H}_2 \xrightarrow{Ni} \text{CH-CH}$$

**Recall the test for chirality**

A carbon is chiral when it has four different groups attached. That means $\text{CH}_2$ is never chiral, $\text{C(CH}_3)_2$ is never chiral, but $\text{CH(CH}_3)$ joined to two different sides of a ring very often is chiral.

**Sort the six alkene carbons**

Look at the substituents on each C=C. Two of the double bonds are of the type CH=C(CH3), so only the $\text{C(CH}_3)$ end can become chiral. One double bond, the top left one, is of the type C=C with two carbon groups on each side, so both ends can become chiral.

**Count new plus existing centres**

From the two CH=C(CH3) bonds we get 1 + 1 = 2 new chiral centres. From the fully substituted C=C bond we get 2 new chiral centres. That is 4 new in total. Y already has one saturated chiral CH where the left ring joins the lower chain, and the $\text{C(CH}_3)_2$ bridge is not chiral. Total = 4 + 1 = 5.

options.A: Correct. Four chiral centres are created on hydrogenation (2 from the fully alkyl substituted double bond, 1 each from the other two double bonds) plus one pre-existing saturated chiral CH gives 5 in the fully saturated product.
options.B: Too high by one. This often comes from counting the quaternary C(CH3)2 carbon as chiral. It has two identical methyl groups so it can never have four different groups, even after saturation.
options.C: Too high. This comes from assuming every alkene carbon (6 carbons) becomes chiral plus one existing centre, then miscounting CH2 groups. Any alkene CH that becomes CH2 after H2 addition has two H atoms and is achiral.
options.D: Much too high. This comes from counting all ring junction carbons and all methyl-bearing carbons as chiral without checking for two identical methyls or two H atoms, and without checking symmetry of the two paths around the ring.
